draft.title: Rounding decimals
card: To round to a given number of decimal places, find the last digit you are keeping. Then look at the digit right after it.
If the next digit is 5 or more, round up: add 1 to the last digit you keep. If it is 4 or less, leave the last digit as it is. Then drop all the digits after it.
Example: round 3.476 to 1 decimal place. The last digit kept is 4. The next digit is 7, so round up. The answer is 3.5.
To check an answer is reasonable, round each number to something easy first. 4.9 × 2.1 is close to 5 × 2 = 10, so an answer of 10.29 is reasonable but 102.9 is not.
draft.remember: Look at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less stays.

a.q: What is 6.382 rounded to 2 decimal places?
a.why: The last digit kept is 8 and the next digit is 2. Since 2 is 4 or less, the 8 stays and the answer is 6.38. Rounding up to 6.39 looks at the wrong digit, as the 8 is not the digit that decides.
a.clue: Only the digit right after the last one you keep decides.

b.q: Ben estimates 7.8 × 4.1 by rounding each number to the nearest whole number first. His calculator shows 31.98. Which estimate shows this answer is reasonable?
b.why: 7.8 rounds to 8 and 4.1 rounds to 4, so the estimate is 8 × 4 = 32. The calculator answer of 31.98 is very close to 32, so it is reasonable. Rounding 7.8 down to 7 is a mistake, because the next digit 8 means round up.
b.clue: Round 7.8 using the digit after the 7.

problems.detail: The question asks which estimate 'shows this answer is reasonable', and only one option ends with 'is reasonable'. The other three all say 31.98 is too small or too large, so a student can pick the right option from the stem's wording alone without doing the estimate.

check.summary: The card, the answers and the explanations are correct. In question b, the right option is the only one that says 'reasonable', matching the question's wording, so it gives the answer away; rewording the stem to 'What does Ben's estimate show?' would fix this.
